Here are several proven strategies that an apartment building can adopt to lower its collective heating costs. You can combine building-physics measures, technical upgrades and operational improvements for best results:

1. Improve the building envelope  
   • Wall insulation – add or upgrade exterior or cavity‐wall insulation to reduce heat losses.  
   • Roof and attic – insulate lofts, attics and flat roofs; consider blown‐in insulation for irregular cavities.  
   • Windows and doors – install high-performance (low-E, argon‐filled) windows or add well-fitted storm windows and weatherstripping to reduce drafts.  
   • Air-tightness – locate and seal cracks around pipe penetrations, service shafts and electrical outlets; use airtight membranes in renovation projects.

2. Upgrade heating and distribution systems  
   • High-efficiency boiler or heat pump – replace old boilers with condensing gas/oil boilers or even better, ground- or air-source heat pumps that achieve COPs of 3–5.

1. Upgrade or Replace the Heat Source

Natural (or passive) ventilation—relying on wind pressures and thermal buoyancy to move air through a building—offers several advantages over fully mechanical systems:

1. Lower energy consumption and operating costs  
   • No or minimal use of fans and motors reduces electricity demand for ventilation.  
   • Reduced running costs over the building’s lifetime, contributing to lower overall energy bills and carbon emissions.

2. Simplicity and reliability  
   • Fewer mechanical components (fans, ducts, controls) mean fewer potential points of failure.  
   • Simpler systems are easier and cheaper to maintain; there are no filters or fans to service regularly.

3. Improved acoustical comfort  
   • No fan noise or rumble from ductwork.  
   • Can contribute to a quieter indoor environment if openings are designed correctly.

4. Enhanced indoor environmental quality  
   • Fresh air enters directly from the outdoors—when properly filtered or controlled, it can promote better air quality

A grid contract (often called a network or “grid access” agreement) and an electricity supply contract are two legally and commercially distinct agreements you need in order to have power in your home or business. Here’s how they differ:

1. Purpose  
   • Grid contract: Governs your right to connect to and use the physical electricity network (poles, cables, transformers, meter). It’s with your local grid operator or distribution company.  
   • Supply contract: Covers the purchase of the electricity commodity itself (the kilowatt-hours you consume). It’s with an electricity retailer or supplier.

2. Who you deal with  
   • Grid contract: A regional grid company appointed for your area. They are responsible for maintaining the lines, meter readings and ensuring voltage quality.  
   • Supply contract: Any licensed electricity supplier you choose. They buy power on the wholesale market (or produce it themselves) and sell it to you.

Control and regulation technology refers to the methods, devices and systems used to monitor, steer and keep technical processes—such as heating, ventilation, air-conditioning (HVAC), lighting or industrial production—within defined set-point values. In the context of buildings or industrial installations it typically comprises the following elements:  
• Sensors and transducers, which measure key parameters (temperature, humidity, flow, pressure, CO₂, occupancy, etc.)  
• Controllers (such as programmable logic controllers – PLCs – or dedicated building-automation controllers), which compare measured values against desired set-points and compute the corrective actions  
• Actuators and final-control elements (valves, dampers, motors, pumps, frequency inverters) that carry out the controller’s commands  
• Regulation algorithms, often based on feedback loops and sometimes incorporating predictive or adaptive strategies (PID control, model-predictive control, fuzzy logic)

In the electric‐vehicle charging world the distinction between “normal” (often called AC) charging and “fast” (generally DC) charging is almost entirely one of power output:

1. Normal (AC) charging  
   – Power levels: typically up to 22 kW  
   – Delivery: Alternating current from the grid is converted inside the vehicle

   – Delivery: Chargers convert grid AC to high-power DC before delivering it directly to the vehicle battery  
   – Typical use case: highway service stations and high-throughput urban hubs where drivers need a large charge in 20–40 minutes

• Prevent overloads on the local electrical installation or upstream grid  
• Make optimal use of the existing supply capacity without costly upgrades  
• Ensure that all connected vehicles receive a fair share of power

In most building‐lighting standards (for example EN 12464-1), stairwells and landings should be designed for a maintained horizontal illuminance of at least 100 lux measured at the walking surface (i.e. on the stair treads and landings). Key points:  
• Recommended average: 100 lx across treads/landings for general use.  
• In higher-risk or public buildings you may choose 150 lx for extra safety and visual comfort.  
• Emergency (backup) lighting along escape routes in stairwells must deliver a minimum of 1 lx at floor level.  
• Uniformity is important—aim for an average-to-minimum ratio (Eavg:Emin) of no more than 1.5:1 to avoid dark spots.

In most multi-dwelling or public buildings the stairwell is treated as an un-occupied but frost-protected space. Swedish building regulations (BBR) and good practice therefore require:  
• A minimum winter temperature of +12 °C in the coldest part of the stairwell (to avoid condensation, mould and frozen pipes).  
• For user comfort and to help smoke control in an escape route, many property managers aim for +15 – 18 °C.  

So, as a rule of thumb:  
– In cold climates keep the stairwell at no less than +12 °C.  
– For a more pleasant experience and better smoke‐layer performance, target around +15 °C (up to +18 °C if your heating system and energy budget allow).
